study.title: Deuteronomy 29 Renewal of the covenant, warning against idolatry and the limits of what was revealed
study.overview: This chapter introduces Moses renewing the covenant with Israel in the plains of Moab, as part of his farewell speech. He recalls the saving acts of the LORD, calls all the people to remain faithful to the covenant and warns with severity against sinful self-confidence and idolatry. The chapter ends by distinguishing between the secret things, which belong to the LORD, and the revealed, which were given for the obedience of the people and their children. The central message is that God's grace sustains the covenant, but the answer required is obedient faithfulness.

outline.title: Remembrance of God's acts and the victories granted
outline.explanation: Moses places the renewal of the covenant in Moab and recalls what Israel saw in Egypt, in the wilderness, and in the defeats of Sehon and Og. The people must recognize that their history was sustained by the action of God, not by self-force.

outline.title: Exhortation to obedience and inclusion of all the people in the covenant
outline.explanation: Israel is summoned to keep and fulfill the words of the covenant to prosper in the way of God. The covenant is publicly presented before the LORD, including leaders, children, women and foreigners residing, and is bound to the promise made to the patriarchs.

outline.title: Danger of idolatry and judgment on hardened heart
outline.explanation: Moses recalls what Israel saw among the nations and forbids any heart that deviates to serve other gods. The false security of those who imagine peace as he persists in sin is denounced, and the text describes the removal under curse of the covenant.

outline.title: Testimony of nations, explanation of exile and the limit of human knowledge
outline.explanation: The generations to come and the people around will ask for the devastation of the earth, and the answer will be the breaking of the covenant and idolatry. The chapter concludes with the assertion that what God has hidden remains with him, while what he revealed was given to be obeyed forever.

study.context: According to the notes, Moab is the region east of the Jordan where this speech was given. The chapter belongs to Moses' farewell speech and resumes the covenant in the form of solemn renewal. Matthew Henry's note highlights that it is a reaffirmation of the already established covenant, and Adam Clarke notes that this initial verse is treated by some as a continuation of the previous chapter in certain Hebrew manuscripts.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter unites grace and responsibility. God leads Israel, preserves it in the wilderness and introduces it into inheritance; this grace bases the call to faithfulness. The covenant is not a mere formalism: it involves all the people, including resident foreigners, and requires concrete obedience. The text also emphasizes the seriousness of idolatry, described as a bitter root that contaminates the community and attracts curse. There is still an important statement about divine providence: not everything will be explained to the human being, but what God has revealed is sufficient and obligatory for obedience. In Protestant evangelical reading, this reinforces that trust in the Lord must be humble, persevering and guided by the revelation received, without irreverent curiosity about the occult.

scholarViews.insight: Moses is closing his farewell speech, reviewing the history of Israel from the exodus and calling the nation to promise allegiance to the LORD; this shows that grace sustains God's relationship with Israel.
Moses, as a mediator, brings together the people for a formal renewal of the covenant, with a solemn appeal to obedience, without turning the moment into a mere external ceremony.

The expression of not having a heart to understand does not need to be read as an accusation of lack of means; it points out that the people did not make faithful use of the advantages and the aid received.

questions: In what ways does this chapter show that Israel's obedience should be born from the memory of God's grace, not fear alone?
What forms of "spiritual self-confidence" or false peace the text denounces when someone imagines to be secure while persisting in sin?
How does the distinction between secret and revealed things help us to deal with difficult questions without abandoning obedience?
study.practice: Examine your fidelity to the light of the history of God's grace in your life: remember what He has already done, reject any idol that is competing with your loyalty and obey what has been clearly revealed in the Scriptures. Instead of trying to control what God has not explained, focus on what He has already commanded to do. It is also worth practicing a community faith: the chapter shows that the covenant reaches the whole house and all the people, then obedience must be taught, remembered and lived publicly and consistently.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow to affirm additional details about date, specific ceremony or geographical context beyond Moab and Moses' final discourse. It is also not possible to safely determine all the nuances of the original Hebrew expressions without resorting to external sources. At some points, commentators differ in tone or emphasis, especially on 29:4 and 29:29.
